A pigeon is here, scratching at the boards, hoping for food. The animal's soft grey form seems out of place in the shifting gloom, and it seems to be oblivious to the nightmare around it.
Something is tied to its scrawny leg. The bird flaps, too nervous for us to detach it. Perhaps if we were to sedate it first?

A fine Beechwood pipe, its bowl polished from years of handling. The stem is wrapped in bands of an exotic metal that appear to reflect more light than they receive.
This was Alfred's most prized possession. Perhaps we might use it to obtain a moment of calm amongst the chaos.
This item can provide ,, and inspiration.

A clothbound collection of withered limbs and body parts. The first victim of the Ash Plague has been collected by Dr Caligar.
The remnants of this mysterious victim might still offer hope for a cure when returned to Caincross Yard.
Although they are unremarkable to look at, these small flowers are renowned for their healing properties. We could process the petals in a laboratory to create a restorative treatment.
An ancient grain, its dry stalks supporting rough spiked ears. Cultivated and cropped with the pretence of making stodgy bread, its less puritan use is for fermenting a strong home-brew liquor.

The Oil bud is a greasy thick-stemmed plant, its wiry branches lined with rows of waxy buds. Engineers and Apothecaries frequently cultivate this plant, crushing its buds for natural lubricant they contain.
A clutch of leathery leaves, the colour of an overcast day. When steeped in boiling water, this herb will result in a brew that can help focus and study.
A creased collection of scribbled pages, ink stained scraps laced in fragments of unknown language and arcane symbology.
A noisy metal bucket that seems to clang and clatter with the slightest provocation. It is stained and dented from years of hauling coal and water.

An intricate master key device from the Venatus Institute. Its slim metal body bristles with ridges and teeth, each protrusion is attached to a rotating band like an ornate puzzle.
We can use this item to help us unlock sealed containers in the mansions archives.
A well-thumbed index from Bleakhurst College, describing the canonical organisation of archives and texts. It should allow us to locate useful items within the organisational chaos of the archives.

A corroded and chipped handbell. It seems ordinary, yet vibrates at the slightest touch, as if resonating with occult energies. When rung, its uncanny chime echoes between the worlds.
This item can be used to summon forth visions of lost souls. But beware, ringing the bell will cause significant damage to the wielders' own sanity.

A miracle of modern technology, this handheld lantern produces its illumination through mechanical means.
A small crank allows the user to charge up an internal battery which powers the device. This allows the lamp to have near unlimited use - just don't get it wet.
With this to aid us we should be able to explore further into the depths of the cellars.
A simple miner's lantern, built from cheap wire and battered metal plates. Its oil reservoir feeds a cracked wick, providing an unstable but vital light source.

A dented and dirt encrusted miners lantern, its workings and wiring clogged with mud and rust.
If we clean it up perhaps we can make it shine again.
A well-used garden spade, made from dark tundra oak and sporting a tempered iron blade. It will dig a little deeper than the trowel we already have.
A crooked trowel, tarnished with age and spotted with rust. The scratched metal blade is dented, but the sharp edge is still strong enough to bite into the frosty soil.

A mecanist lantern from the Venatus workshops. Its clockwork heart produces a hypnotic hum when activated. This soporific sound, combined with a soft scattering of dappled light is guaranteed to induce sleep
The act of sleeping reduces the fatigue of all characters present in the room. It may also provide us with or inspiration.

A collection of poems, written by the controversial author Peter Gwindell.
To many critics, the rambling stanzas and violent imagery appears to be nothing more than provocative posturing.
But to others, the intensity of the writing and its otherworldly tone were a source of great inspiration.
Studying this tome can reward us with ,or inspiration.

A crooked pole and knotted line. Simon's beaten old fishing rod, a gift from some long forgotten friend of the family.
Its main feature is its durability, managing to remain serviceable after years of being used to retrieve paper planes from trees and lift baskets through windows.

An essential part of any fieldwork pack, this sturdy telescope lets the user focus objects at a remarkable distance. Its well oiled mechanism allows it to be stowed efficiently and then extended on demand in the manner of a theatrical pirate.
Under the layers of grime, slime and grit lies what looks to be a well constructed telescope. We should clean this up for a better look.
A pair of ornate binoculars, composed of burnished brass fittings and oil smudged leather. The lenses stain the world a watery blue, but their magnification and focus are impressive.

A collection of dry biscuits, preserved fruit and teabags. None of it is appetizing but none of it is rotten either.

A chunk of meat cut from a trapped hare. Its scrawny flesh might make a decent meal when cooked.

Dear Ms Voltok,
Thank you for your order. Included in this parcel are two 'Somnus Umbra' seeds. They are fully dessicated and should last for years if not decades in their dry form.
If you are to use them for therapeutic aid, we advise rehydrating the kernels in a cup of hot water, and drinking the solution. Consuming the seeds independently would likely cause a more intense and potentially dangerous effect.
Arborist Pilken, Verden Row

Dear Mr Vitali,
We have located and enclosed the seed you requested. It is of the genus 'Somnus Umbra', a cave shrub that thrives in the coves and gullies of the Yarlen inland sea. It is unfortunately the only instance of this type that we can provide at present. However we will contact you should we locate more.
Please Note; although it has been used by primitive cultures as an anaesthetic and soporific we advise against such applications. It is not coincidental that the Yarlen goat population is frequently decimated by incidents of drowning during the seeding season of the plant.
Arborist Pilken, Verden Row

Sophia Ackeron enters the Kitchen looking damp and dejected. She dumps a collection of wet instruments and paperwork on the large oak table and begins to dismantle the casing of an unusual crank-driven device.
The item has clearly been caught in the rainstorm that can still be heard pattering outside. Sophia dries what elements she can reach without troubling the delicate wiring and places the object - along with some equally sodden notes - into a warm alcove behind the stove.
She holds her own hands over the fire for a moment, and then strides from the room, leaving ghostly footprints behind her.

The School Room is a spartan space, its bare boards mottled with ink stains and chalk dust. Sophia Ackeron is attending to the bulky mechanical chair that squats in the centre of the room.
She removes a slim metal pen from her pocket and uses it to reset a button in an awkward recess. The chair begins to hum and whir, its insectile limbs moving into some pre-determined formation. Happy with this result she places the pen on the leather seat and stands up to reset the chair.
The pen rolls into the shadows, falling into a gap in the upholstery. Lady Ackeron does not notice, and after a short pause she gathers the rest of her tools and leaves the room.

The cellars are dank and dripping... The Lady Sophia is here, kneeling in a narrow alcove, hemmed in by mouldering crates and crumbling brickwork
She is placing a sheaf of crumpled paperwork into a mecanist document case.
She places the box onto a decaying shelf and seals it, her fingers scrolling the glinting barrels of its delicate lock.
She slides the box into the shadows, glances around nervously, and heads back towards the light.

It is twilight and Amy is treading carefully through the icy field at the outskirts of the estate.
'Pa?', 'Pa Alfred?' she calls, holding an old flickering lantern ahead of her into the falling dusk.
'I know you're out here, old man! It's late and dinner's on! You don't want it to end up with a plateful of wrinkled peas do you?'
She stumbles briefly, regaining her balance, but the lamp shakes lose from her grip and rolls down a ditch into mud and freezing slime.
The girl curses. 'I'm going back in now, so finish your pipe and come in for tea!'
She heads warily back to the orange glow of the wellhouse before the clouds become lost in the darkening sky.

Writer's Note. I have recently developed an awful nervous condition in my hands. I can hardly grip a pen without suffering excruciating pain. I have therefore decided to use the phonograph in place of my notebooks, until the condition improves.
And specifically, today, I felt I needed to document my encounter with a strange character from Blacksands.
He knocked on the door late one morning, referring to himself only as V. He claimed that, prior to my arrival, his family had loaned a precious heirloom to the household and he wished to have the item back. He begged me to look for the object (an amulet of sorts) in the study or archives, perhaps even in the cellars.
I turned him away of course, but I cannot stop thinking about the matter.

I am recording this entry to document a curious dream or vision I had last night.
A fellow writer recommended I try moonfly extract to ease the pain in my hands. I managed to acquire some at a backstreet chemist in Direwych. I must have miss-measured the dose though, because soon after drinking the stuff I fell into an almost comatose slumber.
What was noteworthy about this sleep is that within it I saw the visitor, V, that I had turned away from the gates last week. Although he did not enter the house in my dream he spent a long time sniffing around the courtyard and wellhouse, like a dog hunting for a buried bone.
Eventually I awoke from my trance with a cry and peering outside could see no trace of the man. Was it truly a vision? Or a premonition? Or simply a hallucination?

I could not resist the draw of the moonfly again. My hands still hurt, and the twin prospect of pain relief and possible visions led me to take another dose.
In a performative act I decided to use the wooden goblet my father gave me, as if the theatre of the ancient relic would lead to more inspiring dreams.
This time, rather than seeing my own estate in the vision, I stood upon a grey shore at the edge of a silent sea. Beyond the rolling dunes lay a garden of nocturnal hatchlings, a place of primordial growth. I was frozen in place and watched as a burning moon smouldered in the distant heavens.
I watched light flicker across the waves, until I eventually awoke, my head filled with wonder. What was that place? I must know!
